walkthroughs.body_html:
Modern Analytical Techniques — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Modern Analytical Techniques brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Modern Analytical Techniques.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which species has the same electron configuration as Ar?
options: Na⁺
Cl⁻
F⁻
Mg²⁺

mcqs.q: Successive ionisation energies of an atom always:
options: Decrease
Stay the same
Increase
Vary randomly

mcqs.q: In an exothermic reaction, what happens energetically with the bonds?
options: The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.
Energy released forming new bonds exceeds energy absorbed breaking existing bonds.
Bond breaking releases energy and bond making absorbs energy.
A positive E°cell means the reaction is exothermic in every case.

mcqs.q: If E°cell for a redox reaction is positive, what does that tell you?
options: A positive E°cell guarantees the reaction will happen rapidly at room temperature.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — but it may still be very slow if kinetic barriers are high.
A positive E°cell means the reaction is exothermic in every case.

mcqs.q: If a reaction has a negative Gibbs free energy change, what does that mean?
options: The reactants get colder because they lose mass as energy.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — it can proceed — but it may still be very slow.
A reaction with negative delta G will always happen quickly.
